triage.name: Aphasia
triage.reason: A language deficit that can be characterized by bedside interview and exam, with localization and stroke workup leading to the diagnosis.

demographics: Most common in middle-aged and older adults because stroke is the leading cause
Can occur at any age when caused by head trauma, brain infection, or brain tumor
Risk parallels that of stroke, so it is more common in populations with high rates of hypertension, diabetes, and vascular disease

risk_factors.text: Prior stroke or transient ischemic attack
Neurodegenerative disease such as Alzheimer disease or frontotemporal dementia
Left-handedness or atypical language dominance (changes which deficits appear)

family_history: Family history of stroke or early cardiovascular disease
risk_medications: Anticoagulants (may increase risk of hemorrhagic stroke)

chief_complaints.text: I can't get my words out
I know what I want to say, but the words come out wrong
I can't understand what people are saying to me
My words get mixed up and I can't find the right one
I can't read or write like I used to
My family says I'm not making sense when I talk

hpi.onset: Sudden when caused by stroke or head injury; gradual over weeks to months when caused by a brain tumor or a progressive neurologic disease
hpi.duration: Acute onset within minutes to hours for vascular causes; insidious and progressive for tumor or neurodegenerative causes
hpi.progression: Often worst right after the event and then improves over weeks to months with therapy; may be stable or steadily worsen if the underlying cause is progressive
hpi.location: Not a bodily location; reflects damage to the language areas of the dominant hemisphere (usually the left side of the brain)
hpi.quality: Difficulty producing words, difficulty understanding language, or both; speech may be effortful and halting or fluent but nonsensical
hpi.severity: Varies from occasional word-finding trouble to loss of nearly all language ability
hpi.timing: Constant; may be more noticeable when tired, stressed, or in noisy settings
relieving: Using gestures, pictures, or a communication device
Having one person speak slowly and simply
Writing or drawing instead of speaking

associated_symptoms.text: Weakness or clumsiness of the right arm, leg, or face
Frustration, irritability, or tearfulness when trying to communicate
Numbness or tingling on one side of the body
Vision changes such as loss of part of the visual field

pertinent_negatives: Fever or stiff neck before the speech problem
Progressive memory loss as the first and main problem
Hearing loss that predates the speech problem
Weakness that comes and goes in minutes and resolves completely
Speech difficulty only when anxious or in social situations

negatives: Progressive memory loss as the main problem
argues_against: Delirium from a toxic or metabolic cause

positives.text: Frustration or irritability when unable to communicate

argues_against: Peripheral hearing loss as the cause of communication difficulty

atypical.how_it_differs: Aphasia is uncommon in children and usually follows head trauma, infection, or a seizure disorder rather than stroke; it may be mistaken for a developmental language delay or for stuttering.
Language deficits may be attributed to dementia or hearing loss, and coexisting cognitive decline can make the aphasia harder to recognize and characterize.
missing_classic_features: Isolated language deficit without memory problems

atypical.how_it_differs: Brain infection or abscess is a more likely cause than in other adults, so fever, headache, and focal neurologic signs may accompany the language problem.

general.mild: Alert, cooperative, and fully interactive; may pause or search for words but communicates effectively with circumlocution
general.moderate: Alert and interactive but noticeably effortful or tangential speech; may need repetition or simplified questions to participate in the exam
general.severe: Alert but communication is markedly limited; may follow only simple one-step commands and relies on gestures or yes/no responses
general.critical: Minimally interactive; little or no meaningful verbal output and inconsistent command following, with exam limited to observation and simple stimuli

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to describe their day or a familiar picture, and listen to the flow, effort, and grammar of speech
findings.finding: Speech that is effortful and halting with sparse output (nonfluent) or fluent but empty and paraphasic (fluent)

findings.maneuver: Show common objects (watch, pen, keys) and ask the patient to name each one
findings.finding: Inability to name objects, with circumlocution, wrong words, or made-up words

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to follow simple then multi-step spoken commands (for example, 'close your eyes', then 'point to the ceiling, then touch your nose')
findings.finding: Difficulty following commands despite adequate hearing and attention

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to repeat a short phrase and then a longer sentence
findings.finding: Impaired repetition of words or sentences

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to read a short sentence aloud and then explain what it means
findings.finding: Difficulty reading aloud or understanding written words

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to write their name and a short sentence
findings.finding: Misspelled, agrammatic, or unintelligible writing

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient their name, where they are, and the date
findings.finding: Oriented to person, place, and time

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to count backward from 20 by 1s or to spell a short word backward
findings.finding: Attention and working memory intact for the patient's age

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to smile, show teeth, and close eyes tightly
findings.finding: Lower facial droop on the right

findings.maneuver: Have the patient hold both arms out with eyes closed for 10 seconds
findings.finding: Downward drift or weakness of the right arm

findings.maneuver: Test strength of hip flexion and knee extension on both sides
findings.finding: Weakness of the right leg

findings.maneuver: Test light touch and pinprick on both arms and legs
findings.finding: Reduced sensation on the right side of the body

findings.maneuver: Test visual fields by confrontation in all four quadrants
findings.finding: Loss of the right visual field in both eyes

findings.maneuver: Listen to the clarity of articulation during speech and ask the patient to say 'pa-ta-ka'
findings.finding: Articulation is clear; errors are in word choice and sentence construction rather than in the mechanical production of sounds

findings.maneuver: Examine pupils, extraocular movements, facial sensation, and hearing
findings.finding: Cranial nerves II, III, IV, VI, and VIII are intact; hearing is adequate for conversational speech

findings.maneuver: Observe a sip of water and check the gag reflex
findings.finding: Swallowing is safe with no coughing or choking

findings.maneuver: Check for neck stiffness and perform Brudzinski and Kernig maneuvers
findings.finding: No neck stiffness or meningeal signs

findings.maneuver: Observe for rest tremor and test finger tapping and rapid alternating movements
findings.finding: No rest tremor, rigidity, or bradykinesia

findings.maneuver: Test finger-to-nose, heel-to-shin, and rapid alternating movements
findings.finding: No limb ataxia or dysmetria

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to hold both arms extended with wrists dorsiflexed for 30 seconds
findings.finding: No flapping tremor of the wrists

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin and check temperature by touch
findings.finding: No rash, petechiae, or warmth suggesting infection

labs.caveat: Both hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia can cause focal deficits and altered language; a point-of-care glucose is checked before any imaging in a suspected stroke.
Reflects chronic glycemic control and vascular risk; not part of the acute stroke decision.
An elevated INR raises the chance of hemorrhagic stroke and must be known before thrombolysis; a normal INR does not exclude it.
Prolonged by heparin or a coagulopathy; relevant when bleeding is a consideration.
Thrombocytopenia increases hemorrhagic risk and is a contraindication to thrombolysis.
Mild leukocytosis is common after acute stroke; marked elevation or a left shift suggests infection such as meningitis or encephalitis.
Needed before contrast CT angiography and to gauge renal reserve; chronic elevation is common in this population.
Hyponatremia can cause confusion and focal deficits that mimic aphasia; correct slowly.
Consider when hepatic encephalopathy is suspected as a cause of altered language and attention.
Thyroid disease can contribute to confusion but rarely causes isolated aphasia.
Only when infection or inflammation is suspected; a pleocytosis supports meningitis or encephalitis rather than stroke.
Elevated in central nervous system infection or inflammation.
Low values suggest bacterial or fungal meningitis.

findings.finding: Irregularly irregular rhythm without distinct P waves, consistent with atrial fibrillation
Sinus rhythm
ST elevation in a territorial distribution suggesting acute myocardial infarction as the embolic source
Left ventricular hypertrophy or other evidence of hypertensive heart disease

Periventricular and cortical atrophy consistent with a neurodegenerative process

No large-vessel occlusion

No significant stenosis

Reduced left ventricular ejection fraction with mural thrombus
Valvular vegetation suggesting endocarditis
Normal study

findings.text: Epileptiform discharges or electrographic seizures over the dominant temporal lobe
Diffuse or focal slowing
Normal background activity

initial.why: Bedside glucose is checked immediately because hypoglycemia and severe hyperglycemia can mimic a stroke and are rapidly reversible
Baseline blood counts and to look for infection or thrombocytopenia
Electrolytes, renal function, and glucose before contrast imaging
Looks for atrial fibrillation or acute myocardial infarction as the embolic source
First-line to exclude hemorrhage and identify a large infarct or mass

initial.test: CT angiography of the head and neck
initial.why: Identifies large-vessel occlusion when thrombectomy is being considered
initial.only_if: the patient may be a candidate for endovascular therapy

initial.why: Most sensitive for acute infarct and for small or posterior lesions
initial.only_if: CT is nondiagnostic or the deficit is unexplained

initial.why: Cell count, protein, and glucose when central nervous system infection or inflammation is suspected
initial.only_if: fever, headache, meningismus, or immunocompromise is present

confirmatory.why: Formal bedside or standardized testing by a speech-language pathologist characterizes the aphasia type and severity

supporting.why: Assesses chronic glycemic control and vascular risk
Cardiovascular risk profile for secondary prevention
Screens for thyroid disease that can contribute to cognitive change
Looks for a cardioembolic source such as atrial thrombus or valvular disease
supporting.only_if: a cardioembolic source is suspected or the stroke is cryptogenic

supporting.why: Screens for carotid stenosis after a transient ischemic attack or minor stroke
supporting.only_if: the event is in the anterior circulation and the patient is a potential revascularization candidate

supporting.why: Evaluates for seizures or nonconvulsive status epilepticus
supporting.only_if: seizure activity or fluctuating language deficits are suspected

not_indicated.why: Not routinely needed for an isolated language deficit
No role in the workup of aphasia unless a urinary infection is suspected as a cause of delirium
Not useful for diagnosing stroke or aphasia
Not relevant to a language deficit
Only when hepatic encephalopathy is suspected, not routinely

decision_points: Check a bedside glucose immediately in any patient with a sudden language deficit
Noncontrast CT head first to exclude hemorrhage before any thrombolysis
If the patient may be a thrombectomy candidate, add CT angiography of the head and neck
MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging when CT is nondiagnostic or the deficit is unexplained
Lumbar puncture only when infection or inflammation is suspected, and after imaging if there is concern for mass effect
Speech-language evaluation confirms the type and severity of aphasia and guides therapy

differential.name: Acute ischemic stroke of the dominant hemisphere
differential.why_considered: Sudden onset of a language deficit in an older adult with vascular risk factors is the most common cause of aphasia
differential.trigger: Abrupt onset of language difficulty within minutes to hours, especially with right-sided weakness or visual field loss

history: Sudden onset, often maximal at the start
Vascular risk factors such as hypertension, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, or smoking
Associated right-sided weakness, numbness, or visual loss
exam: Right-sided facial droop, arm drift, or leg weakness
Nonfluent or fluent aphasia with preserved attention and orientation
labs: Point-of-care glucose normal or only mildly elevated
INR, aPTT, and platelets within range for thrombolysis decisions
imaging: Restricted diffusion in the left inferior frontal or superior temporal gyrus on MRI

differential.name: Intracerebral hemorrhage
differential.why_considered: Sudden language deficit with headache, vomiting, or reduced consciousness can be caused by bleeding into the dominant hemisphere
differential.trigger: Severe headache at onset, vomiting, or rapid decline in consciousness with a language deficit

history: Severe headache at onset
Nausea or vomiting
Anticoagulant use or uncontrolled hypertension
exam: Marked focal deficits such as dense hemiplegia
labs: Elevated INR or prolonged aPTT if anticoagulated
imaging: Hyperdense intraparenchymal hemorrhage on noncontrast CT

differential.name: Hypoglycemia
differential.why_considered: Low blood glucose can cause focal neurologic deficits, including language difficulty, that resolve with correction
differential.trigger: Any patient with a sudden language deficit before glucose is checked, especially if diabetic or on insulin

history: Diabetes treated with insulin or a sulfonylurea
Missed meal, increased activity, or recent dose change
Sweating, tremor, or palpitations before the language problem
exam: Deficit that improves after glucose administration
No focal structural signs on imaging
labs: Resolution of symptoms after glucose correction
imaging: Noncontrast CT head without acute infarct or hemorrhage

differential.name: Delirium
differential.why_considered: Acute confusion with disorganized speech can be mistaken for aphasia, especially in older or hospitalized patients

history: Fluctuating course over hours to days
Recent infection, surgery, medication change, or hospitalization
Inattention as the prominent feature
exam: Speech disorganized but naming and comprehension relatively preserved when attention is captured
labs: Abnormalities suggesting infection, metabolic derangement, or drug effect
Urinalysis or chest imaging may reveal a trigger
imaging: Head imaging without acute focal lesion

differential.name: Dysarthria
differential.why_considered: Slurred or effortful speech can be mistaken for a language problem

history: Speech is hard to understand but the patient knows what they want to say
May be associated with stroke, Parkinson disease, or medication effect
exam: Articulation errors on 'pa-ta-ka' with intact naming, comprehension, and writing
No paraphasic errors or word-finding difficulty
labs: Not diagnostic; used to evaluate underlying cause
imaging: May show lesion in motor pathways rather than language cortex

differential.name: Primary progressive aphasia
differential.why_considered: Gradual, progressive language decline without a sudden event suggests a neurodegenerative cause

history: Insidious onset over months to years
Language difficulty is the first and most prominent problem
Memory and behavior relatively preserved early
exam: Word-finding difficulty or effortful speech without acute focal weakness
imaging: Focal atrophy of the left frontal or temporal lobe on MRI

differential.name: Brain tumor
differential.why_considered: A mass in the dominant hemisphere can cause gradual language difficulty, sometimes with headache or seizures

history: Gradual onset over weeks to months
Headache, seizures, or progressive focal deficits
History of cancer
exam: Language deficit that may fluctuate with edema
labs: Not diagnostic; may show nonspecific findings
imaging: Enhancing mass with surrounding edema on MRI

differential.name: Herpes simplex encephalitis
differential.why_considered: Infection of the temporal lobes can cause fever, headache, and language dysfunction
differential.trigger: Fever, headache, or new seizures with language difficulty, especially in an immunocompromised patient

history: Fever, headache, and malaise before the language problem
Behavioral changes or seizures
Immunocompromised state
imaging: Temporal lobe edema or enhancement on MRI

severity.mild: Occasional word-finding difficulty with preserved ability to communicate; patient is independent and participates fully in conversation
severity.moderate: Noticeable effortful or empty speech; needs repetition or simplified questions; may require some assistance with communication
severity.severe: Marked limitation in language output or comprehension; follows only simple commands; relies on gestures or yes/no responses
severity.critical: Minimal or no meaningful verbal output and inconsistent command following; may be unable to communicate needs or protect the airway

red_flags.meaning: Suggests acute stroke or hemorrhage; requires emergency evaluation and imaging

red_flags.finding: Severe headache, vomiting, or decreased consciousness
red_flags.meaning: Suggests hemorrhage or increased intracranial pressure

red_flags.finding: Fever, neck stiffness, or new seizures
red_flags.meaning: Suggests central nervous system infection such as encephalitis or meningitis

red_flags.finding: Right-sided weakness or visual field loss
red_flags.meaning: Localizes to the dominant hemisphere and supports a structural cause
Hypoglycemia can mimic stroke and must be corrected immediately

complications.name: Aspiration pneumonia
clues: Fever and infiltrate on chest imaging

complications.name: Reduced ability to participate in care
clues: Need for family or caregiver interpretation

special_populations.differences: Aphasia is uncommon and usually follows head trauma, infection, or seizures rather than stroke; may be mistaken for developmental language delay or stuttering.
Language deficits may be attributed to dementia or hearing loss; coexisting cognitive decline can make aphasia harder to recognize and characterize.
Brain infection or abscess is a more likely cause than in other adults; fever, headache, and focal neurologic signs may accompany the language problem.

key_questions.question: When exactly did the speech problem start, and was it sudden or gradual?
key_questions.looking_for: Sudden onset within minutes to hours points to stroke or hemorrhage; gradual onset over weeks to months points to tumor or a neurodegenerative process

key_questions.question: Can you tell me what you want to say but the words won't come out, or do the words come out but not make sense?
key_questions.looking_for: Effortful, sparse output suggests a nonfluent (expressive) aphasia; fluent but empty or nonsensical speech suggests a fluent (receptive) aphasia

key_questions.question: Do you have trouble understanding what people say to you?
key_questions.looking_for: Impaired comprehension localizes toward the posterior superior temporal (Wernicke) region and distinguishes receptive from purely expressive deficits

key_questions.question: Has anyone noticed weakness, numbness, or clumsiness on one side of your body?
key_questions.looking_for: Right-sided weakness, numbness, or facial droop localizes to the dominant (usually left) hemisphere and supports a structural vascular cause

key_questions.question: Did you have a severe headache, vomiting, or lose consciousness when this started?
key_questions.looking_for: Severe headache at onset, vomiting, or decreased consciousness raises concern for intracerebral hemorrhage or raised intracranial pressure

key_questions.question: Have you had any fever, neck stiffness, or new seizures?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever, meningismus, or seizures suggest central nervous system infection such as encephalitis or meningitis rather than stroke

key_questions.question: Have you had a stroke or a transient ischemic attack before?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior stroke or TIA is a strong risk factor and raises the likelihood of a recurrent vascular event

key_questions.question: Do you have high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, or an irregular heartbeat such as atrial fibrillation?
key_questions.looking_for: Vascular risk factors, especially atrial fibrillation, support a cardioembolic or atherosclerotic stroke as the cause

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, especially blood thinners?
key_questions.looking_for: Anticoagulants raise the risk of hemorrhagic stroke and must be known before any thrombolysis; antiplatelets are relevant to vascular risk

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent head injury or a fall?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent trauma suggests a traumatic cause such as contusion or subdural hematoma rather than spontaneous stroke

key_questions.question: Is the problem getting better, staying the same, or getting worse over time?
key_questions.looking_for: Improvement over days to weeks fits a vascular event with recovery; steady worsening fits a tumor or progressive neurodegenerative disease

key_questions.question: Do you have trouble reading or writing as well as speaking?
key_questions.looking_for: Involvement of reading and writing confirms a language disorder rather than an isolated articulation problem

key_questions.question: Do you have trouble swallowing, or do you cough or choke when you eat or drink?
key_questions.looking_for: Dysphagia raises the risk of aspiration and is common with dominant hemisphere strokes

key_questions.question: Has your memory been getting worse over months or years, or is this only about language?
key_questions.looking_for: Progressive memory loss as the main problem suggests dementia; isolated progressive language decline suggests primary progressive aphasia

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, drink alcohol heavily, or have a family history of stroke or early heart disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Modifiable vascular risk factors and family history that inform secondary prevention

reasoning_points: A language disorder affecting production, comprehension, reading, or writing rather than a mechanical articulation problem
Sudden onset in an older adult with vascular risk factors points to an acute ischemic stroke of the dominant hemisphere
Localization to the dominant hemisphere is supported by right-sided weakness, sensory loss, or a right homonymous hemianopia
Attention and orientation are preserved, which argues against delirium as the cause of the language deficit
Articulation is clear on 'pa-ta-ka' with errors in word choice and sentence construction, distinguishing aphasia from dysarthria
Bedside glucose is checked immediately because hypoglycemia can mimic a stroke and is rapidly reversible
Noncontrast CT head excludes hemorrhage before any consideration of thrombolysis
MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging is the most sensitive study for acute infarct when CT is nondiagnostic
Speech-language evaluation characterizes the type and severity of aphasia and guides therapy
Alternative causes such as brain tumor, central nervous system infection, and primary progressive aphasia are considered when the onset is gradual or atypical

Clear right-sided facial droop and arm weakness localizing to the dominant hemisphere
Vascular risk factors such as hypertension and atrial fibrillation
Noncontrast CT without hemorrhage and restricted diffusion on MRI in the left inferior frontal gyrus
medium: Fluent but empty and nonsensical speech with poor comprehension, suggesting a Wernicke-type aphasia
Aphasia without obvious weakness, requiring careful bedside language testing to localize
Coexisting dysarthria or visual field loss that obscures the language deficit
Older adult whose language difficulty is initially attributed to hearing loss or dementia
hard: Gradual onset over weeks to months suggesting tumor or primary progressive aphasia rather than stroke
Fever, headache, and seizures with language difficulty suggesting herpes simplex encephalitis
Patient on anticoagulation with a language deficit and concern for hemorrhagic stroke
Immunocompromised patient with focal language deficit from a brain abscess or infection
Child with language difficulty after head trauma or seizures rather than stroke
Fluctuating language deficits raising concern for nonconvulsive status epilepticus
